cycle_position.summary: Two markets in one: LISTED small lots are abundant (Zillow: 300,000+ lots of <=5 acres listed June 2026, national median $79,000 at 0.57 acres) while ENTITLED, shovel-ready lots are tight in most metros — competition pushes entitled pricing above what pencils for production builders, and MLS-listed land is systematically overpriced by broker/investor activity. The margin lives in taking un-entitled or under-zoned infill through approvals.

cap_rate_ranges.tier: n/a (land is a residual-value asset, not a yield asset)
cap_rate_ranges.note: Underwrite as finished-value minus (build cost + entitlement cost + carry + margin).

supply_demand.value: Listed small-lot supply deep; entitled-lot supply tight; middle-housing zoning reforms (duplex/triplex by-right) keep expanding the infill entitlement envelope city by city.

debt_terms.value: Raw land = cash or seller financing (banks lend little); construction-to-perm once entitled.

small_investor_verdict.entry_vehicle: Infill lots and shells in the SAME rowhouse submarkets as the core strategy (Philadelphia, Baltimore, Richmond), targeting by-right 2-4 unit builds or gut-rehab shells — plus the speculative NoVA data-center-adjacency land watch.
small_investor_verdict.reasoning: Cash buyer advantage is maximal (no financing contingency on land), and every hour spent learning a rowhouse submarket for the multifamily strategy doubles as land-sourcing intelligence. Discipline rule from the sources: never pay MLS ask for land; the deal is off-market or at the tax sale (the PWC delinquency pipeline from the July pass applies directly). Entitlement/permit timeline risk is the tax on the higher margin.

gaps: Middle-housing zoning reform status per target city (DC/Arlington/Alexandria have versions; not systematized into the rules engine yet)
